newsitem.title: FRANCE: France wants China accord on Ariane back-up launch.
newsitem.headline: France wants China accord on Ariane back-up launch.

text.p: France is seeking an agreement with Beijing to allow Europe's Ariane rocket to be used as a back-up in case of failure of China's Long March launcher, the newspaper Le Monde reported on Saturday.
The French minister for post, telecommunications and space, Francois Fillon, will raise the issue on an official visit to China starting on Sunday, the report said.
"The idea is that Arianespace and Great Wall agree a 'back-up' pact: in the case of a failure of a satellite launch on the Long March rocket, Ariane would take over and vice versa," the report said.
The aim is not to transfer valuable European space technology or help China develop its rockets, but make Arianespace more competitive, it said.

Arianespace is the European consortium which operates the Ariane launcher and holds around half the world market for satellite launches. It faces tough U.S. competition from giant Lockheed Martin and a planned merger between Boeing and McDonnell Douglas.
Russia is also active in the launch market.

Arianespace suffered a major setback last June when a new generation Ariane 5 exploded just seconds into its maiden flight from the Kourou launch centre, in French Guiana on the northeast coast of South America.
The China Great Wall Industry Corp launches commercial satellites on its Long March rocket. The Long March has been hit by a spate of spectacular accidents in the last two years.
Last August 18, a Long March 3 rocket failed to put into proper orbit the U.S.-made Chinasat-7 telecommunications satellite.
Last February, a Long March 3B rocket exploded a few seconds after liftoff, killing six people.
In January 1995, six people were killed when a Long March launcher carrying an Apstar 2 satellite blew up.
